title: Teaching on Purpose #14: Actions to Consolidate Understanding
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In the fourteenth installment of his 'Teaching on Purpose' series, Adam Kohlbeck interviews Ashbrook Infant School headteacher Jamie Ainscow about a specific technique for reducing cognitive load during vocabulary instruction: pairing new words with a physical action the whole teaching team agrees to use consistently. The underlying justification is cognitive-load theory — young students have limited processing capacity, and reinforcing a new word's meaning through a repeated, cross-classroom-consistent action frees up working memory for other demands, such as stringing several newly learned words together into a sentence. Kohlbeck and Ainscow are careful to specify boundary conditions rather than presenting the technique as universally applicable: abstract words like 'hope' may benefit more from an icon or symbol than a physical action, and once a word's meaning is secure, continuing to use the action can slow the pace of teaching unnecessarily. The piece situates this single technique within Chiltern Learning Trust's broader framework of six 'core purposes' of teaching, explicitly framing the choice of any technique — including this one — as something that must be 'driven by our purpose and mediated by context,' rather than applied as a fixed classroom routine.
points: The requirement that 'teaching teams decide on the action they will all use for each piece of new vocabulary' turns a single-classroom trick into a school-wide consistency practice, so students encounter the same memory cue for a word across every classroom and context.

Kohlbeck and Ainscow's distinction between concrete words (suited to physical actions) and abstract words like 'hope' (better served by an icon or symbol) shows the technique is not one-size-fits-all, but requires matching the memory aid to the type of concept being taught.

The explicit 'when might you not use' section — dropping the action once understanding is secure, to protect lesson pace — models the kind of purpose-driven, context-sensitive technique selection the whole 'Teaching on Purpose' series is built around, rather than treating any single strategy as a permanent fixture.
quotes: At Chiltern Learning Trust, we have six core purposes that capture everything teachers do: Securing, maintaining and regaining attention; Communicating meaning; Driving hard thinking; Enable and scaffold practice; Utilising memory; Checking for understanding.
When teaching students anything, especially when those students are young, teachers need to do anything possible to support processing.

When a new piece of vocabulary is introduced to a class, teachers might support student processing of the new vocabulary by providing an action that they can repeat each time the word is used to remind students of the word's meaning.
When the word can be understood through a single action, the action serves as a powerful reminder, not just of the word itself but also of the context in which the word was first encountered.
When a word is particularly abstract, such as 'hope', it may be more beneficial to assign an icon, symbol or widget to it.
When student understanding of the meaning of a particular word is secure, they no longer need the action to support their practice.
we need to be driven by our purpose and mediated by context to make sure that we choose the right technique, at the right time for the right reason.
